page.standfirst_html:
Only the 87 proposed fixes need a decision each. The other 135 (emphasis, cleared, out of scope) open pre-set to agree with the verdict: skim them with the Pre-set filter and click only the ones you disagree with. Any click replaces the preset, and the export records which ones you never touched.

Every text flag the comparator raised for the main Appendix: Discussions and Information, adjudicated against P.Appendix.09Feb22.pdf, from a fresh validator run (its counts matched the 2026-09-12 record exactly: 215 flagged sentences, 50 near-certain, 3 missing, 18 reference mismatches, 60% clean).

This pass did not work from the flag list alone. #834 established that dropped source paragraphs clear the missing detector on a loose match elsewhere and surface only as low-similarity noise, so every source page was read top to bottom against the site and its page image opened (PDF pp1, 3, 5–55; pp2, 4 and 56 are blank). Emphasis was compared mechanically from the PDF's font data.

The read-through is what found the worst of it. Day 3's Funnel Experiment discussion (printed pp16–17) is rewritten rather than transcribed: four whole paragraphs and about seven further sentences gone, sentences invented in their place — one of which (“the behaviour of Rule 3 usually isn't dramatic!”) the very next line contradicts — a passage from Activity 3–i duplicated into it, and two invented headings. The validator reported two of those four paragraphs. Activity 9–c has lost its whole second paragraph and Day 1 one more, neither reported as missing.

Elsewhere the pattern is the one #833 found: plausible single-word swaps that invert the sentence. “The bulk of quality” reads “the lack of quality”; “scarily close” reads “surely close”; “about seven times more than” reads “about three times as many with”. Both six-sigma probabilities carry the wrong number of zeros, one making the figure 100× too large. Ed's Red Beads total reads 68 where the source and the arithmetic say 65. Five Deming quotations are quietly altered. git blame puts nearly all of it in the original conversion commit (efb9e8f, #132).

Because of our familiarity with the Ford example, there are no surprises here. Rule 2’s histograms are rather wider than Rule 1’s histograms, matching what was seen to occur in the Ford example. Rule 2 produces more variation than Rule 1. Using the kinds of measures of variation familiar to statisticians, Rule 2’s variation is generally calculated to be around 40% greater on average than that of Rule 1. The automatic compensation device was indeed “tampering” with the system, making things worse rather than improving the system in any way whatsoever.

But beware of “over-analysing” histograms. The eye might be drawn to unusually short bars such as at 30 in Simulation B’s Rule 2 and, even more so, the non-existent bar at 28 in Simulation A’s Rule 1. They mean nothing—just “the luck of the draw”! As I said at the beginning, data by their very nature vary, and just now and again they vary in annoyingly untypical ways.

I imagine that one can still purchase automatic compensation devices. I suppose they may do some good with processes that are horribly unstable. But I think it would be rather less expensive and more sensible to use control charts, thus enabling focus on bringing the processes into statistical control and then using Rule 1 or, better still, get working on improving the process since more will then be known about it.
